pos: n. (proper name; Egyptian servant of Sheshan who married his daughter)
etymology: Egyptian, of uncertain meaning; the Hebrew form is Yarcha'.
biblical_def: Jarha is the Egyptian servant who became the son-in-law and heir of Sheshan of Judah. “Now Sheshan had no sons, but daughters. And Sheshan had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Jarha” (1 Chronicles 2:34). “And Sheshan gave his daughter to Jarha his servant to wife; and she bare him Attai” (1 Chronicles 2:35). Through Attai the line runs on for thirteen generations to Elishama (1 Chronicles 2:36–41), so that an Egyptian servant became a father in the house of Jerahmeel of Judah. The law had said, “thou shalt not abhor an Egyptian; because thou wast a stranger in his land” (Deuteronomy 23:7). Sheshan kept his name alive by joining a stranger to his house, much as Abram once considered Eliezer of Damascus his heir. Jarha is a small picture of the gospel: a servant and a foreigner brought into the family of Judah, given a bride, and made a father of a line. In Christ the stranger is no more a stranger, but a fellow citizen with the saints.

pos: n. (proper name; a Jerahmeelite, son of Jonathan)
etymology: Hebrew Zaza', movement, abundance; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Zaza is a descendant of Jerahmeel of Judah, son of Jonathan. “And the sons of Jonathan; Peleth, and Zaza. These were the sons of Jerahmeel” (1 Chronicles 2:33). The house of Jerahmeel descends from Hezron, the grandson of Judah: “And the sons of Jerahmeel the firstborn of Hezron were, Ram the firstborn, and Bunah, and Oren, and Ozem, and Ahijah” (1 Chronicles 2:25). Zaza's father Jonathan was the son of Jada, and his uncle Jether “died without children” (1 Chronicles 2:32), so the branch continued through Jonathan's sons, Peleth and Zaza. The verse that names Zaza closes the main line of Jerahmeel with the words, “These were the sons of Jerahmeel.” The Jerahmeelites later dwelt in the Negev, and David counted them friends while he was at Ziklag. Zaza is a single name at the end of a branch, but the Chronicler did not let it fall, for God keeps account of every family in the tribe of the King.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Caleb son of Hezron)
etymology: Hebrew Yesher, uprightness, from yashar, to be straight, to be right.
biblical_def: Jesher is the firstborn son of Caleb the son of Hezron by Azubah. “And Caleb the son of Hezron begat children of Azubah his wife, and of Jerioth: her sons are these; Jesher, and Shobab, and Ardon” (1 Chronicles 2:18). This Caleb is the ancestor of the house of Hur and of Bezaleel: “And when Azubah was dead, Caleb took unto him Ephrath, which bare him Hur” (1 Chronicles 2:19). “And Hur begat Uri, and Uri begat Bezaleel” (1 Chronicles 2:20), the craftsman God filled with His Spirit to build the tabernacle. Jesher was the half-brother of Hur, of the line from which the master workman came. His name is the Hebrew for uprightness, the word used of the straight way of the righteous. Nothing more is written of him. The Chronicler begins the house of Caleb with Jesher's name and ends the section with the craftsman of the tabernacle, as if to show that the upright line of Judah was given to the service of God's house.

pos: n. (proper name; a man or town of Judah, son of Tehinnah)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ir Nachash, city of the serpent or city of Nahash, from 'ir, city, and nachash, serpent, bronze.
biblical_def: Irnahash is named in the genealogy of Judah as the son of Tehinnah, and the name is also that of a town. “And Eshton begat Bethrapha, and Paseah, and Tehinnah the father of Irnahash. These are the men of Rechah” (1 Chronicles 4:12). The margin reads “the city of Nahash,” for in these lists “father of” often means founder of a town. The section follows the prayer of Jabez: “Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast” (1 Chronicles 4:10), and the family of Chelub, “And Chelub the brother of Shuah begat Mehir, which was the father of Eshton” (1 Chronicles 4:11). The name may mean city of copper, and some place it near the copper workings of the Arabah. Irnahash is a reminder that the genealogies record towns as well as men, the settling of the land as well as the generations of its people. God gave Judah its cities by families, and the Chronicler kept the record of both.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Eshtemoa in Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Yishbach, he praises or he soothes, from shabach, to praise, to still.
biblical_def: Ishbah is named in Judah's genealogy as the father, or founder, of Eshtemoa. “And the sons of Ezra were, Jether, and Mered, and Epher, and Jalon: and she bare Miriam, and Shammai, and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa” (1 Chronicles 4:17). The next verse explains the household: Mered had two wives, one of Judah, and “Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took” (1 Chronicles 4:18). Ishbah seems to be a son of that Egyptian princess, joined to Judah by marriage. Eshtemoa became a Levitical city: “And Jattir with her suburbs, and Eshtemoa with her suburbs” (Joshua 21:14), and David sent spoil there from Ziklag (1 Samuel 30:28). The son of Pharaoh's daughter founded a town that housed the priests of the LORD and was remembered by David. Ishbah's name means he praises. A daughter of Egypt who joined herself to Judah bore a son whose town served the worship of Israel's God.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Ishi of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Zocheth, strong or proud; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Zoheth is a man of Judah, son of Ishi. “And the sons of Shimon were, Amnon, and Rinnah, Benhanan, and Tilon. And the sons of Ishi were, Zoheth, and Benzoheth” (1 Chronicles 4:20). Benzoheth means son of Zoheth, so the verse may record father and grandson together. The section that follows names the families of Shelah, Judah's third son: “the families of the house of them that wrought fine linen, of the house of Ashbea” (1 Chronicles 4:21), and “the potters, and those that dwelt among plants and hedges: there they dwelt with the king for his work” (1 Chronicles 4:23). Linen weavers and potters, men who served the king with their hands, are recorded in the same breath as the heads of houses. Zoheth's name stands among them, in a chapter that honors ordinary labor done for the king. Every calling in Judah was part of the life of the people from whom the King would come.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Judah of the house of Etam)
etymology: Hebrew Yishma', desolate or he hears; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Ishma is a man of Judah named among the sons of the father of Etam. “And these were of the father of Etam; Jezreel, and Ishma, and Idbash: and the name of their sister was Hazelelponi” (1 Chronicles 4:3). The house descends from Hur, “the firstborn of Ephratah, the father of Bethlehem” (1 Chronicles 4:4). Etam was a town near Bethlehem, later fortified by Rehoboam: “He built even Bethlehem, and Etam, and Tekoa” (2 Chronicles 11:6). Ishma thus belongs to the clans of the Bethlehem country, the district of Ruth and Boaz and David, and of the birth of Christ. The Chronicler names the sons and also their sister, Hazelelponi, an unusual honor in a list of men. Ishma's name may mean he hears. Of all the families around Bethlehem, God knew which would give the world its King; He recorded the others too.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Judah of the house of Etam)
biblical_def: Idbash is a man of Judah named with Ishma and Jezreel among the sons of the father of Etam. “And these were of the father of Etam; Jezreel, and Ishma, and Idbash: and the name of their sister was Hazelelponi” (1 Chronicles 4:3). His name comes from the word for honey, the sweetness of the land that flowed with milk and honey. The house belongs to the clans of Hur, “the firstborn of Ephratah, the father of Bethlehem” (1 Chronicles 4:4). The chapter opens with the sons of Judah: “Pharez, Hezron, and Carmi, and Hur, and Shobal” (1 Chronicles 4:1). Idbash belongs to the country around Bethlehem, where Rehoboam later fortified Etam. The land God gave was sweet, and the Psalmist found God's judgments “sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb” (Psalm 19:10). The man named for honey lived in the land of honey, near the town where the Bread of life would be born.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Ashur and Helah of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Yitschar (written Tsochar), he will shine or tawny; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Jezoar is a son of Ashur, the father of Tekoa, by his wife Helah. “And Ashur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah” (1 Chronicles 4:5). The sons of Naarah are listed first: “And Naarah bare him Ahuzam, and Hepher, and Temeni, and Haahashtari” (1 Chronicles 4:6). Then: “And the sons of Helah were, Zereth, and Jezoar, and Ethnan” (1 Chronicles 4:7). Ashur's town was Tekoa, the home of the wise woman who pleaded for Absalom and of the prophet Amos, the herdman. The verses that follow name Coz and lead to Jabez, whose prayer God granted. Scripture records that Ashur had two wives without approving it; the creation pattern stands. Jezoar's name stands among the households of Tekoa, the town on the edge of the wilderness from which God would one day call a shepherd to prophesy.
